headline: 10 AWS Mistakes to Avoid in Production
summary: Learn the most common AWS misconfigurations that cause production failures, their impact on cost and reliability, and proactive steps to build resilient cloud architectures.

slides.title: 10 AWS Mistakes That Break Production
slides.subtitle: Avoid these pitfalls before your first live deployment
slides.body: Deploying to AWS for the first time? Small misconfigurations can cascade into major outages, security gaps, and runaway costs. This carousel reveals the top 10 mistakes engineers make and how to prevent them.
slides.deep_dive: Production AWS environments differ vastly from dev sandboxes. Real traffic, compliance requirements, and failure domains expose configuration gaps that seem harmless in testing. Understanding these patterns early saves months of firefighting and builds architectural intuition that scales across cloud providers.
slides.key_fact: Most production failures stem from overlooked defaults, not complex architecture flaws.
slides.why_it_matters: Preventing these mistakes reduces MTTR, controls cloud spend, and establishes security baselines from day one.

slides.title: Where AWS Defaults Lead Astray
slides.subtitle: Managed services need explicit hardening
slides.body: AWS provides powerful defaults optimized for ease of use, not production hardening. Services like S3, RDS, and Lambda require deliberate configuration for encryption, access control, and failure isolation.
slides.deep_dive: Think of AWS defaults like a new apartment: it comes with locks, but you must engage them. S3 buckets default to private but allow public policies. RDS instances default to public accessibility. Lambda functions inherit broad permissions. Each service has a 'secure by default' mode that must be activated through explicit configuration — similar to enabling 2FA on every account rather than assuming it's on.
slides.key_fact: Default configurations prioritize developer velocity over production safety.
slides.why_it_matters: Assuming defaults are production-ready is the #1 cause of data exposure and compliance violations.

slides.title: Production Request Flow & Failure Points
slides.subtitle: Trace a request through hardened layers
slides.body: A production request traverses multiple security and reliability boundaries. Each hop represents a configuration decision that affects availability, latency, and blast radius.
slides.deep_dive: Visualize your AWS environment as a castle with concentric walls. The outer wall (WAF/CloudFront) filters malicious traffic. The moat (VPC/Subnets) isolates workloads. The inner keep (Private Subnets) houses compute and data. Each layer requires specific configurations: security groups as gate guards, NACLs as wall reinforcements, and private endpoints as secret passages. Misconfiguring any layer creates a vulnerable gap — like leaving a side door unlocked in a fortress.
slides.key_fact: Defense-in-depth requires intentional configuration at every network layer.
slides.why_it_matters: Single-layer security fails; layered hardening contains breaches.

slides.title: Impact of Misconfigurations on Key Metrics
slides.subtitle: Conceptual impact on reliability and cost
slides.body: Misconfigurations silently degrade SLAs. Unencrypted storage risks compliance fines. Over-permissioned roles expand blast radius. Missing health checks increase MTTR. Each gap compounds non-linearly under load.
slides.deep_dive: Imagine driving a car with misaligned wheels: it runs fine on empty highways but vibrates dangerously at speed. Similarly, a misconfigured RDS instance performs adequately at 100 QPS but suffers connection storms at 10K QPS due to missing connection pooling. An S3 bucket without lifecycle policies costs pennies at 10GB but thousands at 10TB. These aren't linear problems — they're exponential traps that activate under production scale.
slides.key_fact: Configuration gaps remain invisible until production load reveals them.
slides.why_it_matters: Proactive hardening prevents exponential cost and reliability surprises.

slides.title: Operational Burden: DIY vs AWS Managed Services
slides.subtitle: Managed services shift undifferentiated heavy lifting
slides.body: Self-hosting databases, queues, and caches on EC2 gives control but demands 24/7 ops expertise. AWS managed services (RDS, SQS, ElastiCache) automate patching, backups, and scaling — but require correct configuration to realize benefits.
slides.deep_dive: Running PostgreSQL on EC2 is like maintaining your own power generator: you control every component but handle fuel, repairs, and outages alone. RDS is like grid electricity: professionals manage generation, you just wire your house correctly. The catch? You must still install circuit breakers (security groups), ground wires (encryption), and surge protectors (backups). Miswiring managed services defeats their purpose — like plugging a space heater into a frayed extension cord.
slides.key_fact: Managed services reduce ops burden only when configured per best practices.
slides.why_it_matters: Choosing managed services without proper config creates false confidence.

slides.title: 10 Pre-Production Hardening Steps
slides.subtitle: Verify each before go-live
slides.body: Treat this checklist as your pre-flight inspection. Each item addresses a specific failure mode observed in real production incidents. Automate verification in CI/CD pipelines where possible.
slides.deep_dive: Pilots use checklists because human memory fails under pressure. Similarly, engineers forget critical steps during deployment rushes. Codify these checks as automated gates: Terraform policies that reject public S3 buckets, CI jobs that validate IAM least privilege, pre-deploy scripts that confirm multi-AZ deployment. The checklist becomes executable documentation — preventing the 'it worked on my machine' syndrome at 3 AM.
slides.key_fact: Automated guardrails catch misconfigurations before they reach production.
slides.why_it_matters: Checklists transform tribal knowledge into repeatable, auditable processes.
items: Enable encryption at rest & in transit for all data stores
Restrict security groups to least-privilege CIDR blocks
Configure multi-AZ deployment for RDS, ElastiCache, ALB
Set S3 bucket policies to deny public access & enforce SSL
Implement IAM roles with condition keys (not wildcard policies)
Enable CloudTrail logging to centralized, immutable bucket
Configure VPC Flow Logs for network anomaly detection
Set up billing alarms & cost allocation tags
Define RTO/RPO with automated backup validation
Run chaos engineering experiments (AZ failure, latency injection)

slides.title: Start Hardening Your AWS Environment Today
slides.subtitle: Three immediate steps to production readiness
slides.body: Don't wait for an incident. Pick one service, audit its configuration against the checklist, and automate the fix. Incremental hardening compounds into resilient architecture.
slides.deep_dive: Resilience isn't built in a sprint — it's cultivated through consistent, boring discipline. Start with your highest-risk service (usually the database). Enable encryption, verify backups, test failover. Then move to the next layer. Each hardened service reduces blast radius and builds team confidence. Over time, this becomes your organizational immune system: new services inherit hardened patterns by default, and deviations trigger automated alerts. That's how you scale reliability without scaling headcount.
slides.key_fact: Incremental, automated hardening scales better than one-time audits.
slides.why_it_matters: Proactive configuration management is the highest-ROI reliability investment.
takeaways: Audit one critical service this week using the 10-step checklist
Codify one guardrail as a Terraform policy or CI check
Schedule a game day to test failover and observe blast radius
